verses.1: Al-Mizan prefers “bar from” as obstructing people’s faith over merely turning aside, because the later verses concerning fighting and captives support it. It identifies them as the faithless of Mecca and their followers, who persecuted believers and barred them from the Holy Sanctuary. Making their works go astray metaphorically frustrates their effort to erase truth and preserve falsehood rather than letting it attain its intended aim.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes faith in what was sent down to Muḥammad as a qualifying focus, not redundant emphasis, and regards “it is the truth from their Lord” as an aside. Absolution of misdeeds, which obstruct utmost happiness, is joined to setting right their bāl—their condition, state, or heart. Through clemency God both conceals these misdeeds and reforms the faithful in this life and the Hereafter: the True Religion accords with the fiṭrah, and practising this dīn al-fiṭrah brings society’s felicity and hence a felicitous end.
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains the divergent outcomes by the faithless following falsehood and the faithful the truth from their Lord. Only truth is connected to God, so He personally sets the faithful’s condition right; the faithless are merely not guided to felicitous and righteous ends. Human happiness or misery therefore turns on truth or falsehood, while “that” both makes their attributes clear and magnifies the comparison.
verses.4: Al-Mizan confines the encounter to battle: “strike their necks” means killing with swords; after ithkhān—killing or vanquishing many—captives are bound firmly, then either obliged by being freed or enslaved, or ransomed for money or prisoners, until arms are laid down and hostilities cease. This sequence agrees with (8:67), which likewise bars captives before decimation, and is not abrogated by it or by (9:5); the contrary claim wrongly makes a later general text override a particular one. God could have destroyed the faithless directly, but commands fighting to test both groups: the faithful’s obedience is distinguished from sin, while faithless people may repent from falsehood. The promise that those slain in God’s way will not have their deeds wasted is a general rule for those killed in jihād and qitāl, not one confined to Uḥud.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says God guides those slain in His way to felicity and, by forgiving their misdeeds, makes them fit for paradise. In light of (3:169), setting right their affairs gives them a life worthy of presence with their Lord by lifting the separating veil. Majmaʿ al-Bayān alternatively distinguishes reformation in religion and worldly life as the cause from Hereafter comfort as its effect; Al-Mizan instead reads it as explanatory of guidance. Paradise is their destination, and God has acquainted them with it through revelation, glad tidings at death, the grave, the Resurrection, or all these stages.
verses.6: Al-Mizan says God guides those slain in His way to felicity and, by forgiving their misdeeds, makes them fit for paradise. In light of (3:169), setting right their affairs gives them a life worthy of presence with their Lord by lifting the separating veil. Majmaʿ al-Bayān alternatively distinguishes reformation in religion and worldly life as the cause from Hereafter comfort as its effect; Al-Mizan instead reads it as explanatory of guidance. Paradise is their destination, and God has acquainted them with it through revelation, glad tidings at death, the grave, the Resurrection, or all these stages.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says helping God is struggling in His way to support religion and raise truth, rather than seeking power, booty, or displays of prowess. God’s help supplies victory’s conditions—fear in the faithless, misfortunes turned against them, and faithful composure and courage. Making their feet steady is a specific instance after this general help because bravery and morale are conspicuous causes of victory.
verses.8: Al-Mizan contrasts the fate of the faithless with the faithful whom God helps. Taʿs means falling face-down and remaining so; the phrase may be an invocation against them, or a prediction that they will fall and their efforts prove fruitless, since one lying face-down is especially helpless.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies what God sent down as the Qur’an and the teachings and laws revealed to the Prophet, whom people are commanded to obey. The faithless loathe this revelation and disdain following him, which explains why God makes their works fail.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says dammar allāhu ʿalayhim denotes destruction more intense than ihlāk, which concerns a person’s life, family, home, and possessions. The verse threatens those who disbelieve in the Prophet with a punishment like that of former peoples; its plural may indicate their exposure to many possible worldly and otherworldly punishments, though only one will befall them. It may also state a general rule for all faithless people.
verses.11: Al-Mizan takes “that” to encompass help for the faithful, the faithless people’s failure, and their evil fate. Mawlā, a mīm-verbal noun in the sense of walī, signifies both authority, as a master who intervenes in a slave’s affairs, and assistance. God as sovereign leads His servants toward felicity, righteous deeds, paradise, and victory. This protective mastery (mawlawiyyah) belongs only to faithful people within ʿubūdiyyah. Faithless people take idols or their deities as guardians, but God denies them any real guardianship in creation or legislation; hence He helps the faithful and abandons the faithless. Al-Mizan rejects reducing mawlā to “helper” to avoid conflict with (10:30).
verses.12: Al-Mizan sees this comparison as the effect of God’s wilāyah. The faithful pursue truth, faith, and human moral duties, and are therefore guided and admitted to gardens. Faithless people, indifferent to truth and moral responsibility and concerned only with appetites and lusts—eating like cattle whose only aim is consumption—are left to their own devices and to the Fire. God explicitly admits the faithful because this discharges His guardianship and special ʿināyah toward His awliyāʾ; those detached from it receive no such concern.
verses.13: Al-Mizan reads “town” as its inhabitants, as ahlaknāhum indicates, and identifies the town that expelled the Prophet as Mecca. The verse strengthens him, threatens Mecca’s people, and derides their condition: God destroyed many communities stronger than theirs, and none had a helper against Him.
verses.14: Al-Mizan identifies the one standing on a bayyinah from his Lord with the faithful: they follow a logical proof that gives certainty (yaqīn), as befits those who use their intellects and follow truth. The faithless instead are infatuated with evil actions made decorous by Satan and connected with their low desires (ahwāʾ).
verses.15: Al-Mizan presents the verse as expanding the ultimate contrast. Mathal may mean a description of paradise for the muttaqūn, or, more plausibly, a conventional similitude showing a reality too high for mortal description (32:17); taqwā entails faith and righteous deeds. Its streams remain fresh, milk’s flavor does not change, wine delights drinkers, and honey is purified of worldly impurities; all fruits and forgiveness remove sin and every blight from the Hereafter. An implicit comparison asks whether these inhabitants of paradise equal those abiding in the Fire, forced to drink boiling water that cuts their bowels. The claim that this phrase instead explains (47:14) does not fit.
verses.16: Al-Mizan identifies the listeners as faithless people who attend the Prophet’s recitation of the Qur’an and his explanation of religious teachings, then ask knowledgeable Companions what he has said. Their question may seek meaning because pride, conceit, and whims prevent comprehension, may deride him, or may belittle the speech as meaningless; each reading has an element of validity. Sealed hearts and following desires are distinct yet explanatory descriptions: desire follows the seal, while an unsealed heart retains the pure fiṭrah that can understand divine truth.
verses.17: Al-Mizan contrasts the guided with those whose hearts are sealed and who follow desire. Guidance is submission to what a healthy fiṭrah directs toward and following truth; God’s enhancement raises faith’s degrees. Godwariness is the practical opposite of desire, observing prohibitions and avoiding sin. Thus enhanced guidance completes knowledge, and Godwariness completes practice.
verses.18: Al-Mizan reads the question derisively: those who refuse present proof await the Hour for certainty, but it will come suddenly, leaving no time to work; admonition then belongs to recompense rather than action and cannot benefit. Ashrāṭ are marks whose occurrence indicates the thing marked. Its portents may be creation, the human division into righteous and corrupt, and death, which require judgment, or the Prophet as Seal, the splitting of the Moon, and the Qur’an. The verse is therefore a logical argument, and “suddenly” qualifies the Hour’s coming, not their waiting.
verses.19: Al-Mizan reads “know that there is no god except God” as a command to stand firm in Divine Unity after the sūrah’s account of felicity and misery, or after the immediate contrast between sealed hearts and the guided. The Prophet must seek forgiveness for his sin and for faithful men and women so that he and his community are not left with sins like those whose hearts are sealed; God would not command forgiveness to be sought without answering it. God knows their mutaqallab and mathwā—every changing and settled state, motion and rest—so this grounds constancy, repentance, and vigilance; narrower readings are less general.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says the faithful eagerly ask for a new sūrah and its duties, but a definitive, unambiguous sūrah that commands fighting exposes those of weak faith, rather than hypocrites, in the deathbed gaze of extreme fear. “So they deserve!” either describes what befits them or threatens them with what they hate.
verses.21: Al-Mizan chiefly takes “Obedience and upright speech” as an implied statement of their affair: faith means trusting God and saying “We hear and obey.” When fighting is decided, it is better for them to make that speech true by obeying the command. It also allows the phrase to describe the fighting itself as obedience and upright speech, rooted in faith and rational defence of the righteous community. It rejects readings that attach it as an adjective of “sūrah” or as a continuation of the preceding threat.
verses.22: Al-Mizan addresses those with sickness in their hearts directly to intensify the rebuke. Tawallī means turning from God’s Book and its practice, including struggle, back to polytheism and rejection; such a return would bring corruption, bloodshed, plunder, violated honour, and the treatment of kin as carrion-eaters treat a corpse. This explains why obedience is better for them. Reading tawallī as taking political power is far removed from the context.
verses.23: Al-Mizan identifies those cursed as people who cause corruption and mistreat blood relations. God has made them deaf to true speech and blinded them from the true opinion; it is their hearts, rather than their physical eyes, that are blind.
verses.24: Al-Mizan reads the verse as a rebuke to those just described, with the indefinite “hearts” including theirs and those like them. Majmaʿ al-Bayān cites it against the claim that even the Qur’an’s apparent meanings cannot be interpreted without a report or tradition.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains turning one’s back (irtidād ʿalā al-adbār) as the metaphorical abandonment of what one had embraced. Satan’s taswīl makes what excites the low self seem decorous, and his imlāʾ extends their hopes.
verses.26: Al-Mizan says Satan gained power over apostates because they secretly promised people who loathed God’s revelation that they would obey them in some matters. This limited promise signals a person unable safely to give open, complete obedience, waiting instead for fortunes to change; God knows these secret dealings. The context therefore points to hypocrites who confided in the faithless. Interpretations that make the apostates Jews are excluded because they had not believed, while applying it to Jews who promised idolaters assistance requires an unduly difficult sense of apostasy; perhaps another group of hypocrites is meant.
verses.27: Al-Mizan presents the angels striking the faces and backs of apostates as they take their souls as the consequence of their present conduct: after clear guidance, they apostatise and act as they please.
verses.28: Al-Mizan identifies God’s displeasure with the low desires and Satanic seductions that produce disobedience and ruinous sin. His pleasure and displeasure are Attributes of Act (ṣifāt fiʿliyyah), denoting reward and punishment. The angels’ punishment follows because apostates pursued what displeases God and loathed His pleasure, so their deeds failed and no righteous works remain for them.
verses.29: Al-Mizan defines ḍighn or ḍughn as intense hatred. Those with sick hearts are weak in faith and perhaps first inclined to hypocrisy before apostatising after belief; early Islamic history shows a group fitting this course, distinct from people hypocritical from the outset. The verse says they thought God would not bring out their hatred for the Religion and its followers.
verses.30: Al-Mizan says God could mark people with sick hearts so the Prophet recognized them, but that their laḥn already reveals them: speech marked by insinuation and allusion. Rāghib notes that laḥn can also mean blameworthy mispronunciation through neglected iʿrāb, while rhetoricians praise the indirect sense. God knows both their realities and the aims of all deeds, promising recompense to the faithful and warning others.
verses.31: Al-Mizan says the trial through fighting distinguishes those who wage jihād in God’s way and remain steadfast in performing their duties. Their akhbār are deeds insofar as they report on their doers; their appraisal distinguishes righteous from vicious acts. God’s testing makes servants’ condition manifest, not new knowledge for Him, and is an external act of knowledge (ʿilm fiʿlī) rather than part of the Divine Essence (dhāt).
verses.32: Al-Mizan applies the verse to Meccan leaders of misguidance and anyone like them, who bar people from God’s way, defy the Messenger, and show extreme enmity after guidance is clear. Their plotting harms only themselves, not God. Making their works fail therefore means their efforts to destroy religion’s foundations and extinguish God’s light will come to nothing; the alternative of no Hereafter reward is less suited to the context’s encouragement to fight and promise of victory.
verses.33: Al-Mizan reads the command in its warfare context: obey God’s revealed laws and the Messenger’s religious and military commands, and do not invalidate works by withholding from fighting as hypocrites and apostates do. Although invalidating acts can generally include claiming to favour God and His Messenger, conceit (ʿujub), disbelief or hypocrisy, reproachful charity, sins, or major sins, these applications are rejected as the intended reading because the immediate context concerns fighting.
verses.34: Al-Mizan takes the verse as explaining the preceding warning: failure to obey God and the Messenger, through following what displeases God and loathing what pleases Him, can lead to faithlessness and barring God’s way. Those who die in that state will never be forgiven; barring the way means either turning from faith or preventing others from believing.
verses.35: Al-Mizan prohibits weakness and calling for peace with idolaters while the faithful have the upper hand, meaning triumph, in fighting. God’s being with them means His Divine Assistance (naṣr), not His universal sustaining presence (qayūmiyyah), and explains that advantage. He will not stint (witr) their deeds but give their reward in full; the nearby senses of not squandering or wronging them amount to the same. The verse thus promises victory and full recompense if they obey rather than follow the path that ends in permanent loss of forgiveness.
verses.36: Al-Mizan encourages desire for the Hereafter and abstention from a worldly life that is only play and diversion. Faith and Godwariness consist here in obeying God and His Messenger; God then gives their reward without asking for their wealth in return. In context, “wealth” means all their wealth, as the next verse confirms.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains that if God demanded all their wealth and pressed them for it, their love of it would make them refuse, expose the hatred in their hearts, and lead them astray. Pressing means putting someone under pressure, while stinginess means refusing to give.
verses.38: Al-Mizan argues that being asked to spend only some wealth already shows that some are stingy; if all were demanded, all would be so. The stingy withhold goodness only from themselves, because God needs nothing and asks spending for their own worldly and otherworldly good. Thus God is the All-sufficient and they are needy. If they turn away, He will replace them with people unlike them, who attain faith, Godwariness, and spending in His way.
